slides.title: Cryptographic, Misconfiguration, and Mobile Vulnerabilities
points: This lesson focuses on weaknesses caused by bad cryptography, insecure settings, mobile security restrictions being bypassed, and flaws with no available fix yet.
Security+ Objective 2.3: explain various types of vulnerabilities.

slides.title: Cryptographic
slides.teach: A weakness caused by poor algorithm choice, weak keys, insecure implementation, or misuse of cryptography.

course.learn: A weakness caused by poor algorithm choice, weak keys, insecure implementation, or misuse of cryptography.

breakdown.explanation: The cryptography itself is weak or used incorrectly.
Weak cipher, Hardcoded key, Improper certificate validation

course.why: Strong systems can still fail if crypto choices or implementations are weak.
course.example: An application uses an obsolete cipher with a hardcoded key.
course.exam: Weak cipher / bad key handling → CRYPTOGRAPHIC.
course.check_q: Which category fits an obsolete cipher or hardcoded key?

slides.title: Misconfiguration
slides.teach: A security weakness caused by incorrect, insecure, or unintended configuration settings.

course.learn: A security weakness caused by incorrect, insecure, or unintended configuration settings.

breakdown.explanation: The product may be secure, but the settings are wrong.
Public storage bucket, Excessive permissions, Debug mode enabled

course.why: Incorrect settings can expose otherwise secure technology.
course.example: A cloud bucket is accidentally made public.
course.check_q: Which category fits a secure product configured unsafely?

slides.title: Side Loading
slides.teach: Installing an application from a source outside the official or approved application store or management channel.

course.learn: Installing an application from a source outside the official or approved application store or management channel.

breakdown.explanation: Install an app from somewhere other than the approved store.
Manual APK install, Unapproved app package

course.why: Unapproved sources may bypass vetting and introduce malicious or risky applications.
course.example: An employee manually installs an APK downloaded from a website.
course.exam: Install outside approved store → SIDE LOADING.
course.check_q: What is installing an app outside the approved store called?

slides.title: Jailbreaking
slides.teach: Removing or bypassing manufacturer restrictions on a mobile device to gain greater control or elevated access.

course.learn: Removing or bypassing manufacturer restrictions on a mobile device to gain greater control or elevated access.

breakdown.explanation: The device's built-in restrictions are intentionally removed.

course.why: Jailbreaking weakens platform security boundaries and can allow untrusted software or elevated access.
course.example: A phone is rooted to gain unrestricted system access.
course.check_q: What is bypassing mobile platform restrictions called?

slides.title: Zero-day
slides.teach: A vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor or is being exploited before an effective fix is available.

course.learn: A vulnerability that is unknown to the vendor or is being exploited before an effective fix is available.

breakdown.explanation: Attackers have a usable flaw before defenders have an effective patch.
Unknown browser flaw, Unpatched newly discovered bug

course.why: Defenders may have limited signatures, patches, or mitigations when exploitation begins.
course.example: Attackers exploit a browser flaw before the vendor releases a patch.
course.exam: No effective fix available yet → ZERO-DAY.
course.check_q: Which term describes exploitation before an effective fix is available?

blocks.title: Cryptographic, Misconfiguration, and Mobile Vulnerabilities
blocks.prompt: Focus on the exact failure mode and distinguish it from similar vulnerability categories.

blocks.title: Common exam traps
rows: Weak crypto itself vs. secure technology configured incorrectly
Installing outside approved store vs. removing device restrictions
A flaw is not zero-day merely because it is new; the key clue is exploitation before an effective fix is available

blocks.title: Cryptographic, configuration, and mobile exam shortcuts
items: Weak cipher / bad key handling → CRYPTOGRAPHIC
The weakness is in the cryptographic choice or implementation itself.
Example: An application uses an obsolete cipher or hardcoded encryption key.
The technology may be secure by design, but the configuration exposes it.
Example: A cloud bucket is accidentally configured for public access.
Install outside approved store → SIDE LOADING
The user bypasses the normal application distribution channel.
Example: An employee manually installs an APK downloaded from a website.
The device's built-in manufacturer restrictions are intentionally bypassed.
Example: A phone is rooted to gain unrestricted system access.
No effective fix available yet → ZERO-DAY
The exam clue is not simply 'new'; it is that exploitation occurs before defenders have an effective vendor fix.
Example: Attackers exploit a browser flaw before a patch is released.
blocks.example: Memory: Crypto = weak algorithm/key handling · Misconfig = wrong settings · Side load = outside store · Jailbreak = remove restrictions · Zero-day = no fix yet.

questions.q: An application uses an obsolete cipher even though its permissions and other settings are correct. Which vulnerability category best fits?
questions.explanation: The weakness comes from the cryptographic algorithm choice itself.

questions.q: A cloud service is secure by design, but an administrator accidentally makes a sensitive storage bucket public. Which category best fits?
questions.explanation: The technology is configured insecurely; the problem is the settings.

questions.q: An employee installs an Android app directly from an APK downloaded from a website rather than the approved store. Which vulnerability category is this?
questions.explanation: The application is installed outside the approved distribution channel.

questions.q: A user removes manufacturer restrictions to gain elevated control over a mobile device. Which vulnerability category is this?
questions.explanation: Jailbreaking bypasses built-in mobile platform restrictions.

questions.q: Attackers are exploiting a newly discovered browser flaw before the vendor has an effective patch available. Which term best fits?
questions.explanation: The key clue is active exploitation before an effective fix is available.

questions.q: A mobile app uses strong modern cryptography, but the developer hardcodes the encryption key in the application. Which category best fits?
questions.explanation: Hardcoded key handling is a cryptographic weakness.
